source_question.stem: When a polynomial $P(x)$ is divided by a linear divisor $(x - a)$, the division algorithm states $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + R$. Which statement explains why the remainder $R$ must be identically equal to the constant value $P(a)$?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the quotient $Q(x)$ must be equal to zero for all real values of $x$.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the linear divisor $(x - a)$ must always be equal to $1$.

options.label: C
options.text: Because $P(x)$ can only have positive integer coefficients.

options.label: D
options.text: Because the degree of $R$ must be strictly less than the degree of $(x - a)$, forcing $R$ to be a constant, and evaluating at $x = a$ annihilates the term $(a - a)Q(a) = 0$.

answer.value: Because the degree of R must be strictly less than the degree of (x - a), forcing R to be a constant, and evaluating at x = a annihilates the term (a - a)Q(a) = 0

hint_ladder.hint1_conceptual_nudge: Consider the degree condition imposed on the remainder $R$ by the division algorithm when dividing by a degree-1 polynomial.
hint_ladder.hint2_tactical_step: Substitute $x = a$ into the identity $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + R$ and observe what happens to the product $(x - a)Q(x)$.

distractor_rationales.opt-A: Student confuses the quotient polynomial with the remainder.
distractor_rationales.opt-B: Student confuses divisor expression with unity.
distractor_rationales.opt-C: Student confuses domain restriction with algorithmic division constraints.

core1a.title: Polynomial Division and Remainder Invariance
core1a.concept: For any polynomial division P(x) = D(x)Q(x) + R(x), deg(R) < deg(D). When deg(D) = 1, deg(R) = 0, so R is a constant. Evaluating at the root of D(x) = 0 annihilates the quotient term, leaving P(a) = R.
core1a.boundary_conditions: If divisor is quadratic or higher, remainder is generally a polynomial of degree >= 1, so P(a) alone does not yield the complete remainder.

core1b.prediction_prompt: What is the degree of the remainder when a polynomial is divided by a linear polynomial of degree 1?
scaffold_steps: Recall the division algorithm degree inequality
Deduce remainder is a constant of degree 0

html_representation:
When a polynomial $P(x)$ is divided by a linear divisor $(x - a)$, the division algorithm states $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + R$. Which statement explains why the remainder $R$ must be identically equal to the constant value $P(a)$?

Consider the degree condition imposed on the remainder $R$ by the division algorithm when dividing by a degree-1 polynomial.

Substitute $x = a$ into the identity $P(x) = (x - a)Q(x) + R$ and observe what happens to the product $(x - a)Q(x)$.

Review Remainder Theorem
Show Complete Solution

In polynomial division, $\text{deg}(R) < \text{deg}(x - a) = 1$, which forces $\text{deg}(R) = 0$ (a constant $R$).

Evaluating both sides at $x = a$: $P(a) = (a - a)Q(a) + R = 0 \cdot Q(a) + R = R$. Hence $R = P(a)$.
